UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                        )
 PJM Interconnection, L.LC.                             )               Docket No. ER26-1479-000
                                                        )
                                                        )
                                                        )

                                      PROTEST OF VISTRA CORP.

          Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby submits this protest to

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) compliance filing filed on February 23, 2026, in the above-

captioned docket. 2 On December 18, 2025, this Commission issued a landmark Order on Show

Cause Proceedings,3 which established a clear and principled roadmap for the development of co-

located facilities in PJM in a manner that ensures both the reliability and affordability of the PJM

system.      The Commission’s order clearly delineated a path for enabling the expeditious

development and interconnection of co-located facilities. This action was a critical step toward

facilitating the development of digital infrastructure in PJM—the single most important region of

the country for data centers and the other infrastructure necessary to develop and maintain our

world-leading artificial intelligence capabilities.

    Accepting PJM’s compliance filing would be a step backward from the progress made in that

order. Where the Commission required clarity, PJM has proposed ambiguity by failing to propose




    1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).
    2
     PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open
Access Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et al., Docket No. ER26-
1479-000 (filed Feb. 23, 2026) (“PJM Compliance Filing”).
    3
        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order on Show Cause Proceedings”).
 a clear transition mechanism to apply to the facilities that have diligently pursued and, in some

cases, completed, the necessary study process. Similarly, where the Commission mandated speed,

PJM has chosen delay, by proposing a June 1, 2029 effective date for the new transmission services

and a revised necessary study process that would appear to not even begin until 2029—a lifetime

when it comes to digital infrastructure. Collectively, these two elements, unless changed, could

delay integration of co-location configurations until the early 2030s. And where the Commission

required pragmatism, PJM has responded with a truly byzantine proposal for Capacity

Interconnection Rights (“CIRs”) that is clear as mud and appears likely to limit backup resources’

ability to support resource adequacy where they can. To realize the potential of the December

Order, the Commission should direct PJM to file a further compliance that resolves these

fundamental flaws, as discussed further below.

I.         PJM Has Not Demonstrated That the Proposed Revisions to the Necessary Study
           Process Are Just and Reasonable

           In its Order on Show Cause Proceedings, the Commission found the PJM tariff is unjust

and unreasonable because it lacks sufficient clarity and consistency regarding how interconnection

customers can serve co-located load using existing generating facilities. 4 As a remedy, the

Commission directed PJM to clarify that the necessary study process can facilitate the addition of

co-located load behind the meter of an existing generating facility, and to propose tariff revisions

to more clearly describe that process and the scope of the analysis PJM performs in such instances.5

PJM’s tariff revisions therefore must provide sufficient clarity and transparency on the steps




     4
         Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 225.
     5
     Id. PP 226-27. The Commission directed PJM to describe the information that the interconnection customer
must provide about the co-located load for purposes of the necessary study. Id. P 227.

                                                   -2-
 needed for an existing generator to serve co-located load to remedy the unjust and unreasonable

ambiguity in PJM’s tariff.6

         PJM’s proposal falls well short of providing the clarity necessary to remedy PJM’s tariff

in several respects. Specifically, PJM’s proposal does not: (a) contain a transition mechanism or

otherwise address necessary studies that are already in progress or completed; (b) specify how

PJM will calculate and study changes to CIRs; or (c) explain why existing customers with older

interconnection agreements must sign an entirely new version of interconnection agreement before

serving co-located load. Rather than adding clarity, PJM’s proposal introduces new sources of

ambiguity that will cause additional delays and further hinder efforts to add co -located load and

power digital infrastructure in PJM.

         A.      PJM’s Proposal Fails to Include a Transition Mechanism for Customers
                 Already in the Necessary Study Process

         Although some existing generators have worked diligently to pursue co -location

arrangements with large load customers via PJM’s existing necessary study process, PJM’s

proposal would ignore those efforts altogether and press reset on significant commercial

opportunities for large load customers. Indeed, PJM’s proposal does not acknowledge that some

existing generators have already executed necessary study agreements and even received study

results, much less address whether and how the proposed tariff revisions apply to such customers.




   6
       Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 229.

                                                 -3-
 This is a critical issue in this proceeding, given the Commission’s emphasis on facilitating speed

to power,7 and PJM’s replacement rate must directly address that issue to pass muster. 8

          Without any clear transition mechanism, PJM’s proposal could be read to require parties

that have completed the necessary study process to restart that process entirely. In this way, PJM’s

proposal will create further delays for parties that have already sought to pursue co-location

arrangements because those parties will have no way to preserve in-progress or completed

necessary studies. Such delays are not only unnecessary but simply incompatible with the nation’s

urgent need for computing power. That result is also incompatible with the Commission’s Order

on Show Cause Proceedings, which indicated that this compliance filing should memorialize

PJM’s existing approach to necessary studies, but that any “enhance[ment]” to the necessary study

process should occur in a future section 205 filing. 9 There should be no need for parties that are

already in the necessary study process to start over if the tariff revisions at issue here are limited

to complying with the Commission’s directives. Furthermore, requiring generators with executed

necessary study agreements to restart the process violates the rights of those existing generators

that relied on the existing rules to pursue facility modifications for co-location opportunities. 10

          Further, by failing to provide a transition mechanism, PJM’s proposal represents an

unexplained and unjustified departure from the Commission’s customary approach to



    7
      See Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 200 (acknowledging that co-location
arrangements can allow existing generating facilities to begin serving new large co-located loads rapidly and directing
PJM to create a new interim, non-firm transmission service to facilitate more rapid interconnection and operation of
co-located loads); see also id. (Rosner, Comm’r, concurring at P 11) (discussing how the new interim transmission
service leverages speed).
    8
     See Affirmed Energy, LLC v. FERC, 166 F.4th 1070,1079 (D.C. Cir. 2026) (“An agency’s decision is arbitrary
and capricious if the agency entirely fails to consider an important aspect of the problem before it or ignores the
reasonable reliance interests of regulated parties.”).
    9
        Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 227.
     PJM Power Providers Grp. v. FERC, 96 F.4th 390, 400 (3d Cir. 2024) (“P3”) (explaining that the Commission
    10

may not take actions that alter the legal consequences attached to past actions).

                                                        -4-
 interconnection reforms, in which the Commission regularly requires transition mechanisms to

avoid disruption and stranded capital investments. Most recently, in Order No. 2023, the

Commission required transmission providers to (i) tender an interconnection agreement to any

customer that had received a final facilities study report before commencing transitional studies, 11

and (ii) allow late-stage interconnection customers that had already been tendered a facilities study

agreement to opt to continue under a serial study process. 12 The Commission explained that doing

so appropriately respected the investments and expectations of interconnection customers at an

advanced stage in the existing process. 13 And the Commission has consistently employed these

types of transition mechanisms since it first created the standardized interconnection procedures

in Order No. 2003, where the Commission allowed interconnection customers with executed study

agreements to choose to continue under those existing processes or transition processes.14

           Given the Commission’s longstanding approach to interconnection reform, PJM’s

compliance proposal is flawed. PJM does not justify its failure to include a transition mechanism,

let alone acknowledge that there are generators with executed necessary study agreements on file

with the Commission. Thus, PJM has not provided the Commission with the justification it would

need to accept PJM’s proposal and depart from precedent requiring a transition mechanism for




    11
        Improvements to Generator Interconnection Procs. & Agreements, Order No. 2023, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054, at
P 865, order on reh’g, 185 FERC ¶ 61,063 (2023), order on reh’g, Order No. 2023-A, 186 FERC ¶ 61,199, errata
notice, 188 FERC ¶ 61,134 (2024)).
    12
         Order No. 2023, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054 at PP 855, 865.
    13
         Id. P 856.
    14
       Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements & Procs., Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103, at
P 186 (2003), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220, order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-B, 109 FERC
¶ 61,287 (2004), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d sub nom. Nat’l Ass’n of Regul.
Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007); see also Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, 164 FERC ¶
61,234, at P 21 (2018); Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, 158 FERC ¶ 61,003, at PP 45, 59 (2017); Midcontinent
Indep. Sys. Operator, 166 FERC ¶ 61,187, at P 107 (2019); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 167 FERC ¶ 61,275, at PP 19, 39
(2019); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162, at P 60 (2022).

                                                     -5-
 interconnection reforms. 15 And by failing to include a transition mechanism that respects executed

necessary study agreements on file with the Commission, PJM’s proposal appears to render those

filed agreements a nullity, in violation of the filed rate doctrine.16

         Requiring generators with executed necessary study agreements on file with the

Commission to restart the entire process would undermine the central goal of this proceeding: to

expeditiously facilitate the co-location of generation and load in PJM.17 And the delay caused by

requiring generators to restart the necessary study process is further compounded by the fact that

PJM is seeking a June 1, 2029 effective date for the new transmission services, and will seek a

corresponding effective date for the revisions at issue in this proceeding.18 As Vistra will describe



      15
         See F.C.C. v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009) (“An agency may not . . . depart from a
prior policy sub silentio or simply disregard rules that are still on the books. And of course the agency must show that
there are good reasons for the new policy.” (citations omitted)). In the Order on Show Cause Proceedings, the
Commission indicated that PJM should formalize and clarify its existing necessary study process rather than make
substantive changes. See Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 227. To the extent PJM is
seeking to make wholesale substantive changes to the necessary study process, such as by requiring generators that
have already completed the process to start the process again, it must propose such changes in a future section 205
proceeding rather than in this docket. See id. (“To the extent that PJM seeks to enhance the necessary study process .
. . PJM may submit such enhancements in an FPA section 205 filing.”).
    16
       The filed rate doctrine “bind[s] regulated entities to charge only the rates filed with FERC and to change their
rates only prospectively.” Okla. Gas & Elec. Co. v. FERC, 11 F.4th 821, 829 (D.C. Cir. 2021). It applies not just to
rates, but also to matters directly affecting rates. P3, 96 F.4th at 394. Existing necessary study agreements on file
with the Commission are filed rates for purposes of the filed rate doctrine, and those agreements state that their terms
cannot be changed without the consent of the parties. See, e.g., PJM SA No. 7476, Necessary Studies Agreement
between PJM and LSP Digital (0.0.0), § 21 (“This Agreement, or any part thereof, may not be amended, modified, or
waived other than by a writing signed by all Parties.”). Were PJM to require parties with existing necessary study
agreements to enter new agreements, this would impermissibly alter the legal consequences that attached when those
parties initially filed executed necessary agreements with the Commission. See P3, 96 F.4th at 394. And nullifying
necessary study agreements would be patently unfair, as parties that have already paid for necessary studies would
have to pay a second time for the same studies.
    17
        Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 200 (“[T]o facilitate more rapid interconnection
and operation of Co-Located Loads . . . . [W]e direct PJM to submit, within 60 days of the date of issuance of this
order, a compliance filing to create a new interim, non-firm transmission.”)); Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193
FERC ¶ 61,217 (Chang, Comm’r concurring at P 3) (explaining that the “order represents the first step to developing
a package of solutions to address co-location in the PJM footprint” and that the Commission “will assess how [the]
rates, terms, and conditions facilitate the efficient interconnection of co -located loads”).
    18
        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et. al, at
79 (filed Feb. 23, 2026) (“PJM Paper Hearing Initial Brief”). In this proceeding, PJM proposed a 12/31/9998 effective
date, which it indicated it will update to align with the effective date set in the paper hearing. PJM Compliance Filing
at 35.

                                                         -6-
 further in its paper hearing brief, PJM has not shown that this lengthy delay is just and reasonable.

PJM’s attempts to defend that delay based on its capacity market schedule and the need for

software updates are unpersuasive. First, the 3-year forward capacity market schedule cannot

justify a delay in the provision of non-firm, non-capacity backed transmission products. The

capacity market schedule should not delay the provision of firm transmission products either, for

that matter, given that the forecasts used in the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 BRAs included the new

large loads that are likely to come online in that timeframe. 19 Second, PJM has not explained why

it will take until 2029 to update its software to accommodate the new curtailment logic—or why

it cannot provide a transition process in the meantime to serve customers that agree to not pull

energy from the grid and therefore will not need to be curtailed.

          Compounding the delay, PJM indicated that it will seek a corresponding effective date for

the tariff revisions in this proceeding, 20 meaning that PJM’s new necessary study procedures and

new pro forma necessary study agreement would not be effective until halfway through 2029.

That means that customers may need to wait until 2029 to even submit a request to begin the new

necessary study process. Moreover, the pro forma necessary study agreement sets forth a study

timeline of 270 days, with no consequences for study delays.21 In other words, between the study

process itself and the construction of any necessary network upgrades, it is likely that no existing

forecast/2026-load-report.pdf.

         PJM Compliance Filing at 35.
    21
      Id., Attach. A (Revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff) at Part IX, Subpart G (Form of
Necessary Studies Agreement), § 5 (“Proposed Tariff Revisions”).

                                                       -7-
 generator could add co-located load under PJM’s proposed process until 2030 or 2031. PJM’s

proposal is, in effect, a 3- to 5-year moratorium on co-locating large loads with existing generators.

That kind of delay in powering digital infrastructure—via the service option (i.e., co-location) that

will bring speed-to-power faster than any other—is both unnecessary and directly contrary to the

Administration’s efforts to ensure that the nation “has the power needed to win the global artificial

intelligence [] race while continuing to meet growing demand for affordable, reliable and secure

energy.”22

           B.         PJM Has Not Demonstrated That Its Proposal for Delisting CIRs Is Just,
                      Reasonable, and Not Unduly Discriminatory, or That It Is Consistent with the
                      Commission’s Compliance Directives

           In the Order on Show Cause Proceedings, the Commission explained that “an existing

generating facility may not begin serving Co-Located Load that is not Network Load until it has

delisted its CIRs for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve any Co-Located

Load that is not receiving NITS.”23 The Commission also directed PJM to propose tariff revisions

to clarify how the necessary study process works, including with regards to CIR reductions. 24

           While PJM claims that its proposed tariff revisions “promote clarity” by memorializing

this directive,25 PJM’s proposed language, in fact, perpetuates the very ambiguity that the

Commission found renders the tariff unjust and unreasonable. 26 PJM would require existing

generators that seek to add co-located load to submit to PJM “the amount of reduction to Capacity




    22
      Press Release, Dep’t of Energy, Energy Department Launches Speed to Power Initiative, Accelerating Large-
Scale Grid Infrastructure Projects (Sept. 18, 2025), https://www.energy.gov/articles/energy-department-launches-
speed-power-initiative-accelerating-large-scale-grid.
    23
         Order on Show Cause Proceedings, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 230 (emphasis added).
    24
         Id. P 226.
    25
         PJM Compliance Filing at 26 n.83.
    26

                                                     -8-
 Interconnection Rights to facilitate the Co-Located Load configuration.”27 PJM’s necessary study

will then “assess the impact of the reduction in Capacity Interconnection Rights.” 28 But PJM does

not explain how a generator should calculate the amount of the reduction of its CIRs, nor does it

clarify how PJM will assess the impact of that reduction. Without these critical details, PJM’s

tariff remains ambiguous—the exact issue the Commission sought to remedy in this proceeding.

                      1.       PJM’s Proposal Is Impermissibly Vague Regarding How to Calculate
                               CIR Reductions and Could Be Interpreted in an Unduly
                               Discriminatory Manner

           PJM has failed to address the Commission’s directive to “clarify its interconnection

procedures and agreements to ensure that it is clear to both new and existing Interconnection

Customers how to interconnect in a Co-Location Arrangement.”29 Instead, PJM’s proposal would

require existing generators to provide PJM with “the amount of reduction to Capacity

Interconnection Rights to facilitate the Co-Located Load configuration,” a mandate that is

inappropriately vague and could potentially be read to sweep far too broadly.30 Concerningly,

PJM’s revisions could be read to require generators to include in their CIR reduction calculation

any portion of a facility that will ever provide power to a co-located load. That would mean that

      Proposed Tariff Revisions at Part VIII, Subpart A, section 401 (Applications for Cyle Process), § H(3)(b)(i)(c).
PJM identifies the language memorializing the Commission’s directive as located in “proposed revisions to Tariff,
Part VII, Subpart A, section 401.H.3.a – b.” PJM Compliance Filing at 26 n.83. PJM’s proposed revisions do not
include changes to Part VII of the tariff. We assume PJM intended to reference Part VIII, but if that is the case, PJM
must clarify as much in a future filing.
    28
         Proposed Tariff Revisions at Part VIII, Subpart A, section 401 (Applications for Cyle Process), § H(3)(b)(ii).
    29

Initial Brief attaches illustrative tariff language that states, “[t]he Eligible Customer must designate the individual Co-
Located Generating Facility that will serve the individual Co-Located Load . . . and provide the megawatt level of
energy from the Co-Located Generating Facility dedicated to serving the Co-Located Load.” PJM Paper Hearing
Initial Brief, Attach. A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI, Subpart B, section 711.1. PJM does not mention
the illustrative language in this proceeding, but even if PJM intended for the illustrative language to guide calculation
of the CIR reductions, which is something PJM has not indicated, it would not cure the ambiguity in PJM’s proposed
revisions because the language does not explain what it means to be “dedicated to serv[e]” co -located load.
    30
         Proposed Tariff Revisions at Part VIII, Subpart A, section 401 (Applications for Cyle Process), § H(3)(b)(i)(c).

                                                          -9-
 a two-unit generator using one 50 MW unit to serve co-located load and one 50 MW unit to serve

the grid while providing occasional, interruptible backup service to the co -located load would need

to delist 100 MWs of CIRs. In other words, PJM’s proposal could potentially treat this two-unit

configuration the same as a generator that serves 100 MW of co-located load, despite the fact that

each configuration provides different amounts of capacity to the grid. And if read in that manner,

PJM’s proposal could require generators to delist more CIRs than those associated with the

“portion” of the facility that is actually dedicated to providing firm service to a co-located load.

         Clarity is needed to ensure that the tariff language is not read in such a broad manner. A

broad reading that would require units that provide only occasional, interruptible energy to co-

located load to delist their CIRs would deprive ratepayers of generation that is generally available

to serve the grid when needed and risk unnecessarily increasing capacity prices. Allowing

secondary units providing occasional, interruptible service to co-located load to retain their CIRs

would also be consistent with other requirements in the PJM tariff. PJM’s capacity market must-

offer rules excuse generators with a “financially and physically firm commitment to an external

sale of [their] capacity” from the obligation to offer capacity into PJM’s market. 31 No such

exception applies for generators with a non-firm commitment to sell outside of PJM.                       By

distinguishing between firm and non-firm sales, PJM’s tariff recognizes that firm energy sales pose

unique concerns for capacity market commitments, while generators providing non -firm energy

sales can be expected to perform in the capacity market. The same distinction applies to generators

that serve co-located loads: primary units that provide firm energy to a co -located load clearly

       PJM Interconnection L.L.C., Open Access Transmission Tariff, Attach. DD.6, § 6.6 (Offer Requirement for
Capacity Resources) (3.0.0), §§ 6.6 (a), (g); see also PJM Interconnection L.L.C., Constellation Request for
Clarification or, in the Alternative, Rehearing, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et. al, at 4 (filed Jan. 20, 2026).

                                                   - 10 -
 cannot also provide capacity, but secondary units that provide only occasional, interruptible energy

to co-located load can.

           It would also be unduly discriminatory to require secondary units that occasionally serve

co-located load on an interruptible basis to delist their CIRs. As PJM recently explained, it allows

generators that export energy outside of PJM on a non-firm or recallable basis to function as

capacity resources.32 Those resources must still comply with their capacity obligations, including

the requirement to bid into the day-ahead market.33 But where the generator is not committed in

the day-ahead market, they are not required to “sit idle.” 34 Interruptible backup units in a co-

located configuration should receive the same treatment. As Vistra has previously explained,

secondary units that occasionally provide interruptible back-up service to a co-located load can

fulfill capacity obligations and be expected to perform when needed.35 Indeed, there are

commercial arrangements and associated energy offer rules that would allow such units to both be

available to serve the grid during emergency conditions, while also serving as a back-up to the co-

located load. There is no principled basis to treat an interruptible backup unit in a co-located

configuration differently from recallable exports. But PJM’s proposal for calculating CIR

reductions could do just that, if read too broadly. The Commission should reject vague tariff

 language that could be read in an unduly discriminatory manner and could artificially restrict

capacity in PJM.

          Finally, as a matter of policy, there is simply no reason to ignore the valuable contribution

of back-up units that only occasionally serve co-located load, as capacity resources that help the

region achieve its resource adequacy needs. Ignoring those MWs will force PJM to procure

additional MWs that truly are not needed and will ultimately add significant costs for ratepayers.

                    2.       PJM Does Not Explain How It Will Study the Impact of a Reduction
                             in CIRs

          PJM’s necessary study process aims to “determine whether a planned modification . . . will

have a permanent material impact on the Transmission System.”36 While some of PJM’s proposed

revisions are consistent with that aim, PJM’s proposal also indicates that PJM will “assess the

impact of the reduction in CIRs associated with the Co-Located Load and Co-Located Load

Generating Facility,”37 which could be interpreted to expand the scope of the necessary study

process beyond what it is designed to consider. By failing to explain how it will “assess the impact

of the reduction of CIRs,” PJM appears to provide itself discretion to improperly shoehorn resource

adequacy considerations into the necessary study process. Vistra does not believe it is PJM’s intent

to incorporate a resource adequacy assessment into its necessary study process, as such would be

both inconsistent with its long-standing practice for conducting such studies, and FERC’s

December Order. But PJM’s filing has introduced unnecessary ambiguity, and clarity is needed.

          Studying resource adequacy in the necessary study process would be inconsistent with the

purpose of the necessary study process, which is designed to evaluate the impacts of a change to




   36
        PJM Compliance Filing at 27 n.87.
   37
        Proposed Tariff Revisions at Part VIII, Subpart A, section 401 (Applications for Cyle Process), § H(3).

                                                     - 12 -
 an interconnection on the transmission system. Its goal is to address engineering concerns and

identify transmission network upgrades needed to accommodate the modification, not address

PJM-wide policy issues beyond the scope of interconnection service. And it is unclear how PJM

would have the authority to consider resource adequacy issues in the necessary study process given

that PJM cannot require a generator to sell its capacity into PJM’s market.38

          It would also be unduly discriminatory to consider resource adequacy in the necessary

study process for existing generators that are required to delist CIRs but not for other similarly

situated interconnection customers, because resource adequacy considerations associated with

large load interconnection are not unique to co-location.39 For example, a retiring generator would

have the same impact on capacity prices as a generator that delists CIRs to serve co -located load

because the capacity market would incorporate either change as a shift in the supply curve.

Similarly, a new large load seeking to co-locate would have a similar (but lower) capacity price

impact as a new large load seeking to connect in front-of-the-meter.40 In both cases, the retiring

generator and front-of-the-meter large load would impact capacity prices in a manner similar to a

generator seeking to co-located as load, such that these entities are all similarly situated with

respect to their impact on the capacity market.41 It would therefore be unduly discriminatory to

 consider resource adequacy only for the interconnection of co-located load and not for these other

scenarios that have a similar (or more significant) impact on capacity prices.

         C. PJM Has Not Justified the Requirement to Update Old Generator
            Interconnection Agreements or Explained How the Requirement Will Work in
            Practice

         Other aspects of PJM’s proposal appear to be entirely unresponsive to the Commission’s

compliance directives, would inject further ambiguity into the tariff, and could slow down the

necessary study process and the integration of new large loads.

II.         PJM’s Proposal to Use of “Point of Change in Ownership” Versus “Point of
            Interconnection” in Co-Located Load Definition Creates New Opportunities for
            Undue Discrimination

            In the Order on Show Cause Proceedings, the Commission defined co-located load as a

“configuration [that] refers to end-use customer load that is physically connected to the facilities

of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the interconnection customer’s side of the Point of

Interconnection to the PJM Transmission System.” 52 The Commission correctly reasoned that this

definition is proper because it “reflects the fact that the Co-Location Arrangement is physically

connected to and synchronized to the transmission system” and that “this relationship, and

specifically the interconnection of the generator to the transmission system, is critical to the

determinations” that the Commission made in its Order on Show Cause Proceedings.53 The

Commission directed PJM to incorporate this definition into its tariff. 54

            The Commission should reject PJM’s proposal to revise the Commission’s definition of

co-located load to refer to “Point of Change in Ownership” (“POCO”) instead of “Point of

Interconnection” (“POI”).55 The change in term breeds uncertainty and creates an opportunity for

transmission owners to unduly discriminate against certain customers because the transmission

owners retain significantly more control over the designation of the POCO compared to the POI.

in unduly discriminatory ways because there are no consistent or reliable standards by which the

III.         Conclusion

             PJM’s compliance proposal threatens to impose a 3- to 5-year moratorium on co-location

and thereby throttle the development of digital infrastructure at the very moment that the nation

needs to rapidly build and energize the computing power needed to win the AI race. In the Order

on Show Cause Proceedings, the Commission gave PJM straightforward directions for how it must

revise its tariff to ensure that existing interconnection customers seeking to serve co-located

understand their responsibilities. Rather than follow those directions for clarifying the necessary

study process, PJM inexplicably veered in the opposite direction with its compliance filing, by

impeding co-location opportunities and muddying the waters to make it even more challenging for

interconnection customers to discern how to revise their existing interconnection agreements to

serve co-located loads. The Commission must reject PJM’s counterproductive proposal and ensure

that PJM complies with the Commission’s clear and common-sense mandates from the Order on

Show Cause Proceedings.
